question: How do Messed Up Dress Up, and the way it is being made, compare with the adventure-game engines and editors of the late 1980s and early 1990s (Sierra's AGI and SCI, LucasArts' SCUMM, and the Hugo games): what did they have that we have again, what made their making hard, which of those difficulties we meet again now, and which of ours are new?
engines: Pictures stored as drawing commands (lines and fills), replayed onto a visible screen and an invisible priority screen at once; the priority screen in 12 bands (colours 4 to 15) saying what is in front, and control lines (colours 0 to 3, black a wall) saying where one may walk. 16 colours.
In-house tools; today's fans draw AGI pictures with Lance Ewing's PicEdit, whose priority view shows the bands and lines
Sierra On-Line, 1988; SCI1 from King's Quest V, 1990

SCI0 kept the vector pictures (320 by 190) and the priority screen, and added a control image (white a wall). SCI1 brought 256-colour VGA and pictures painted by hand and scanned in, with an icon interface. King's Quest V wanted 640 KB of memory and 1.2 MB floppy disks; a 16-colour edition was made for weaker PCs.
In-house picture, view and room tools
Lucasfilm Games and LucasArts, 1987 (Maniac Mansion, on the Commodore 64) to 1998

A scripting language and its interpreter (SPUTM), redesigned from one game to the next (again for Indiana Jones, again from scratch for The Secret of Monkey Island). Rooms with walk boxes; iMUSE (1991), music that branches and loops at markers to follow the player. Left in 1998 for GrimE, with Lua.
Verbs and pointing; walking to a click

FLEM placed and named the objects in a room and set clipping planes; MMUCUS compiled a room and its objects into one file, so scripters could change things without rebuilding the room; SPIT for fonts; BYLE, then CYST, for animating and scaling the characters
Gray Design Associates (David P. Gray), 1990 to 1991, shareware
Hugo's House of Horrors and its sequels: a graphic adventure with a typed parser, much like Sierra's AGI games; the DOS version free to share.
Its own engine (called Hugo in ScummVM)
footnotes: Other engines of the era, named here from memory and not checked against sources for this report: Westwood's engine for The Legend of Kyrandia, Revolution's Virtual Theatre (Lure of the Temptress, Beneath a Steel Sky), Coktel Vision's Gob engine, Adventure Soft's AGOS (Simon the Sorcerer), and, later, Adventure Game Studio (1997).
rows: What stands in front of what
AGI's priority screen, in 12 bands, painted with the picture; SCI's priority screen

Every thing standing in a place is an object with a depth, and the friend is drawn behind whatever stands nearer than their feet (ticket 99); since today, what hangs on walls and lies on floors is an object too, always behind the friend (ticket 284)
same
Where one may walk
AGI's control lines; SCI's control image; SCUMM's walk boxes
Collision boxes for walls and what stands; the back line (refined in ticket 310); pits and trap doors that keep the feet out
same
Getting there
SCUMM: walking to a click was in the point-and-click design from the start
👆 Walk where you click (ticket 251) plans a path round what stands in the way; the controller on the screen; real game controllers
same
Rooms and what is in them
FLEM placed and named objects in a room; MMUCUS made quick changes possible without rebuilding the room
📦 placing any thing in any place; 🔬 Inspection's list of a place's objects; 🗺️ World design's grid of places joined by their ways
same, but live
The pictures
AGI: drawing commands, replayed; SCI1: painted by hand and scanned (from 1990)
Drawings written as code (SVG), as AGI's were, so every part of a picture can be a setting, an object, placed or hidden; the picture archive keeps every version
AGI's way, taken further
Music
SCI0: a sound's samples at most 64 KB; iMUSE (1991): music that follows the player
🎵 the music designer; the scenes' movements (swaying, flickering) kept in time with the tune's LFOs
same idea, new form
Slow machines
640 KB, floppy disks, a 16-colour edition of King's Quest V for weaker PCs
60 frames a second first (the black laptop, the iPad): a slow computer shows the places as still pictures while the friend moves (ticket 164); costly effects off unless switched on (⚙️ Advanced)
same
Many platforms
Ports to the Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Mac, FM Towns
Browsers, which differ: today's trap doors swung in Chrome and not in Firefox (ticket 322); computers, tablets and phones
same
The engine changing under the games
SCUMM rebuilt for Indiana Jones and again for Monkey Island; SCI0 to SCI1
232 versions in a week (0.0.1 on 2026-10-12), each live within minutes
same, much faster
Knowing how it all works
Much of SCUMM undocumented; new hires spent a week at "SCUMM University"
agent-instructions.md, kept in step with every change; the dashboard of tickets; this series of reports
same need, written down
Playtesting
Testers, then players, months later
The players are the designers: M and N try a version the afternoon they asked for it; checks run on GitHub's computers after each release
new
new: M and N ask for a thing (a moss, a boulder lever, a bubble that bursts into smaller ones), and it is in the game that afternoon. In 1990 a design was decided by a designer, built for a year, and met players on floppy disks.
The programmer works from their words.
An AI (Claude) writes the code from what Matthew relays, in plain words, and releases it; Matthew decides. The cost of trying an idea is minutes, so ideas get tried rather than argued about.
The game is its own editor.
FLEM and MMUCUS were tools beside a compiled game; 🏞️ Background and 🗺️ World design are the running game, and a change shows at once in the picture the player is in.
The game is a web page; a release is a push, live in about a minute, on any computer with a browser.
Since today, everything a place draws is meant to be an object you can see in 🔬 Inspection, hide and place elsewhere (ticket 284); a picture's settings decide it exactly, seeds included (ticket 274).
Dress Up is where Hazel's user-defined livelits are tried first: what works here, as the best experience when nothing stands in the way, is then built in Hazel.
hugo: Typing ("get key", "open door") to a parser, as in Sierra's AGI games
Pointing, walking, dragging; a game controller; no typing
A haunted house, in EGA pictures
Houses, a castle of rooms, woods, the sea and more, drawn with depth and movement
Find Penelope in the house, by solving its puzzles; an ending
None yet: you dress up a friend and go where you like
An inventory, used on the puzzles
Cooks, a smith, a witch, a healer, who work but do not talk
Yes: places, things, a world, music
next: an inventory, and using a thing on a thing (a key on a door, a bucket on a fire), the oldest machinery of these games
levers, trap doors and boulders (ticket 323) wired to a goal in a place ("get the crown out of the trap room")
🔬 Inspection showing a place's depths and where one may walk as Sierra's priority and control screens did, and 🏞️ Background letting a designer paint them
the cooks, the witch and the healer answering, the player choosing what to say
a world with a goal and a way to finish it, set in 🗺️ World design
small scripts ("when the friend picks up the key, open the door"), in the game first, then as Hazel livelits, as SCUMM's scripts were to its rooms
a world saved as a file another player can open, as shareware once passed from hand to hand
unknown: How SCUMM's walk boxes were drawn and stored: the sources found name them (ScummVM fixes them for the Commodore 64 Maniac Mansion) but do not describe the tools.
Sierra's own scanning pipeline for the painted VGA backgrounds: the sources describe it only in general (a 2015 trailer; an art director's biography).
The footnote engines above: named from memory, not checked.

editor_note: I appreciate getting reminded that we don't have all of the ingredients of a game, or even a game maker, yet. We need more ability to script events, add special items with special events attached, and write a story that the NP[C]s help create -- they are still just standins for that. Thank you.
